feedback: If the learner counts cube-by-cube, prompt them to find one full layer first and then iterate it for the number of layers.
If the prediction and the filled count differ, ask them to recount a single layer and recheck the number of layers to locate the error.
If they write cm² or omit the unit, point to one filling cube: volume counts cubes, so the unit is cubic (cm³).
activities.intendedInsight: Measuring volume means counting all the unit cubes that fill the solid. Organising them into layers (one layer multiplied by the number of layers) is more reliable and efficient than counting one-by-one, and counting only the visible faces misses hidden cubes. The unit is 'cubes', so it is recorded in cubic units.
learnerActions: Fill a small open box (or transparent container) whose inside length, width and height are whole numbers of centimetres with centimetre cubes so they pack in snugly, leaving no gaps.
Find the number of cubes in the bottom layer (for a 4 by 3 base, count 4×3 = 12).
Count how many identical layers stack to fill the box (e.g. 2 layers), then add 12 for each layer: 12, 24.
Write the volume with its unit: 24 cm³. State explicitly why it is cm³ and not cm².
Predict the count before filling, then check by filling; investigate any mismatch to find double-counted or missed cubes.
activities.title: Fill a box and count by layers

feedback: If the learner only adds cubes on the three visible faces, ask what is behind and underneath this solid (and, in larger solids, inside), and have them rebuild it layer by layer (physically if possible).
If they over-count, point out that edge and corner cubes belong to only one layer and should be counted once; shading each counted layer prevents this.
If the unit is wrong, relate cm³ to a single filling cube.
activities.intendedInsight: A flat drawing of a solid hides cubes at the back and underneath (and fully interior cubes in larger solids); a reliable count reconstructs the full array by layers rather than tallying the cubes visible on the faces.
learnerActions: Study an isometric drawing of a cuboid built from centimetre cubes (e.g. 4 by 3 by 2).

Identify which cubes are occluded from this single view (at the back and underneath) that the drawing does not show directly, and describe how you know they are there; note that larger solids also contain fully interior cubes a view cannot show.
Count by layers: state the cubes in one layer, then multiply or add across the number of layers to reach the total.
Shade or mark each layer as you count it so no cube is counted twice on a shared edge or corner.
Record the total with the correct cubic unit and explain your reasoning.
activities.title: Count the hidden cubes in a drawing

feedback: If the learner confuses cm² and cm³, have them point to one square (covers a surface) and one cube (fills a space) and match each to area versus volume.
Confirm that the unit must name the same cube that was counted (centimetre cube → cm³).
activities.intendedInsight: Volume is counted in unit cubes, so it is recorded in cubic units; this notation is distinct from the square units used for area.
learnerActions: Given several measured counts, write each volume with the correct cubic unit (cm³, in³, ft³) to match the cube used.
Explain the difference between cm² (area, covering a flat surface with squares) and cm³ (volume, filling a space with cubes).
Spot and correct deliberately mislabelled answers such as '24 cm²' for a volume.
Describe in words why volume is measured in cubic units.
activities.title: Cubic units versus square units
